subject: zoology_2
question_text: Describe the structure of the heart of man with the help of neat labelled diagram.

verification.note: Sourced from 'My Baby Bullet-Q — Senior Inter Zoology' (Star-Q Pass Track Series, Sri Publishers, 2022), book pp.10-11, LAQ 1. The printed exam years are the book's claim, reproduced here as appearances. Zoology-II holds only ONE source book in the corpus, so the two-book union check is structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is our reading of the question and is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

steps.label: Pericardium
steps.why: The heart beats about once a second for a lifetime, so it needs a lubricated bag around it or the friction would wear it away.
common_mistakes: Writing that the pericardium is a single membrane. It is double walled.
Leaving out the pericardial fluid. That is where the mark is.
steps.memory_tip: A double bag with fluid between: the heart slides, never rubs.
steps.margin_note: Open with what the heart is, then take the four parts in order.
lines: The human heart is a hollow, muscular, cone
shaped, pulsating organ between the lungs.
It is about the size of a clenched fist.
It has four parts: pericardium, heart wall,
external structure and internal structure.
The heart is covered by a double walled
pericardium. The outer layer is fibrous and
the inner layer is serous.
Between them is pericardial fluid, which
reduces friction and lets the heart move
freely.

steps.label: Heart wall
steps.why: The middle layer is the thick muscle that does the pumping; the layers on either side of it are only linings.
common_mistakes: Giving two layers. There are three.
Swapping the names. Epi- is outer, endo- is inner.
steps.memory_tip: Epi outside, myo the muscle, endo the inner lining.
steps.margin_note: Three named layers, one line. An easy mark.
lines: The heart wall has 3 layers:
outer epicardium, middle myocardium and
inner endocardium.

steps.label: External structure
steps.why: The grooves on the outside mark exactly where the chambers meet inside, so the outside tells you the inside plan.
common_mistakes: Calling the upper chambers ventricles. The upper pair are the atria.
Leaving out the coronary sulcus. It is the marked groove.
steps.memory_tip: Two small on top, two large below, a groove between them.
steps.margin_note: Five short numbered points cover this mark.
lines: The heart has four chambers.
The two small upper chambers are the atria,
left and right.
The two large lower chambers are the
ventricles, left and right.
A deep transverse groove, the coronary
sulcus, separates atria from ventricles.
Each atrium has an ear lobe like projection
called the auricular appendix.
Two interventricular grooves hold the
coronary arteries.

steps.label: Atria
steps.why: The atria only push blood down into the ventricles a few centimetres, so their walls stay thin.
common_mistakes: Writing that the atria are thick walled. They are thin walled.
Confusing foramen ovale with fossa ovalis. The pore is in the foetus, the scar in the adult.
steps.memory_tip: Foramen ovale is the hole in the foetus, fossa ovalis the mark left behind.
steps.margin_note: The internal structure has four parts. This is the first.
lines: The internal structure has 4 parts: atria,
ventricles, nodal tissue and aortic arches.
Atria are thin walled blood receiving
chambers. The right one is larger.
A thin inter-atrial septum separates them.
In the foetal heart this septum has a pore
called the foramen ovale.
In the adult it is closed and leaves a mark
called the fossa ovalis.

steps.label: Ventricles
steps.why: The left ventricle drives blood round the whole body while the right one reaches only the lungs, so the left wall is the thicker of the two.
common_mistakes: Writing that both ventricles have equal walls. The left is thicker.
Mixing up the two valves. Bicuspid is left, tricuspid is right.
steps.memory_tip: Left works harder, so the left wall is thicker. LAB RAT: Left Atrium Bicuspid, Right Atrium Tricuspid.
steps.margin_note: Name columnae carneae, papillary muscles and chordae tendineae.
lines: Ventricles are thick walled pumping
chambers, separated by the inter-
ventricular septum.
The wall of the left ventricle is thicker
than that of the right.
Their inner surface is raised into muscular
ridges called columnae carneae.
Large conical ridges are the papillary
muscles.
Chordae tendineae are collagen cords that
join the papillary muscles to the bicuspid
and tricuspid valves.

steps.label: Nodal tissue
steps.why: The heart beats on its own because part of its muscle has become tissue that makes its own electrical signal.
common_mistakes: Calling nodal tissue nerve tissue. It is modified heart muscle.
Placing the SAN in the left atrium. It lies in the right atrium.
steps.memory_tip: SAN starts the beat, AVN relays it through the bundle of His.
steps.margin_note: Both nodes with their positions, then the bundle.
lines: It is modified heart muscle, made of two
nodes and fibres.
The sinoatrial node, SAN, lies in the right
upper corner of the right atrium, close to
the opening of the superior vena cava.
The atrioventricular node, AVN, lies in the
lower left corner of the right atrium, near
the opening of the coronary sinus.
The AVN forms the bundle of His, which
divides into right and left bundle branches.

steps.label: Aortic arches
steps.why: The two arches keep the two circulations apart: one carries blood to the lungs, the other to the body.
common_mistakes: Writing that the pulmonary arch carries oxygenated blood. It carries deoxygenated blood.
Starting the systemic arch from the right ventricle. It leaves the left.
steps.memory_tip: Pulmonary from the right to the lungs; systemic from the left to the body.
steps.margin_note: Name the valve at each opening. Those are marked words.
lines: There are two aortic arches in man.
The pulmonary arch arises from the left
anterior angle of the right ventricle. Its
opening is guarded by the pulmonary valve
and it carries deoxygenated blood to the
lungs.
The systemic arch arises from the left
ventricle. Its opening is guarded by the
aortic valve and it carries oxygenated
blood to all parts of the body.

steps.label: Diagram — internal structure
steps.why: A section through the heart is the only view that shows all four chambers, both valves and the great vessels at once.
common_mistakes: Drawing the outside of the heart. The question needs the internal structure.
Leaving the valves out. Bicuspid and tricuspid are expected labels.
Drawing it small. Use about a third of the page.
steps.memory_tip: Outline, then septum, then the four chambers, then the valves, then the vessels.
steps.margin_note: Draw it large and label at least ten parts.

Step 4 — the muscular ridges of the ventricle wall

insider_note: Eight marks, eight headings. Write the four parts as numbered headings first — an examiner marking a wall of prose cannot find the seven points, and the diagram alone carries the eighth mark.
